overview.body: This is an ENHANCE unit! You'll build your first module, function_library.py, and hand the dice to Python. Then Texas gets a say: a coin decides whether you go where you chose, and hazards pop up on the road.

mentorQuote.quote: Random makes a game fun and makes testing hard. This week you learn both halves: how to make things random, and how to pin them down so you can test every single outcome on purpose. The second half is the one employers ask about.

objectives: Write your first module: three functions with docstrings and a self-test
Import your library and call its functions from your game
Add the Destination Gate and hazards with random numbers
Pin random values and test every outcome on purpose
overview.keyConceptsText: Chapter 5 Sections: 5.2 to 5.5 (Defining and Calling Functions), 5.7 (Passing Arguments), 5.8 (Global Constants), 5.9 (Value-Returning Functions: Generating Random Numbers), 5.10 (Writing Your Own Value-Returning Functions), 5.11 (The math Module and modules), 5.12 (Storing Functions in Modules)
overview.textbookReference: Starting Out with Python, 6th Edition by Tony Gaddis, Chapter 5: Functions

testingPins.intro: A pin swaps a random line for a fixed value, so a test comes out the same every time. Comment out the line in the second column and put the line from the third column right under it, at the same indent. When a test needs a different value (like roll = 5), it says so. To restore a pin, delete the fixed line and take the # off the original.
testingPins.restore: Every pin MUST be restored before you submit: CodeGrade runs the random lines itself, with its own fixed numbers.

content.body: Two files this lab. lab-2-2.py starts as your finished Lab 2.1. function_library.py is new: a module, a file of functions your game imports and calls. In this checkpoint it gets its first function, flip_coin(), and a short self-test so you can try it on its own.

A function is a named block of code you can call whenever you need it. Putting the game's dice and coin in their own file means every later lab can use them without copying them, and you can test them by themselves. The library grows all semester; by Module 4 it holds more than a dozen functions.

content.quote: Every team I've worked on has a utils file. It's where the small, boring, reliable things live, so the main program can read like a story. Your library starts with a coin. Treat it like production code anyway: docstrings, clean style, a test you can run any time.

items: Leave two empty lines, then add a section banner and the first function. random.randint(1, 2) picks 1 or 2; 1 means HEADS:

content.code:
# ============================================================
# RANDOM FUNCTIONS (Added in Lab 2-2)
# ============================================================

def flip_coin():
    """
    Flip a coin and return the result.

    Returns:
        str: 'HEADS' or 'TAILS'
    """
    result = random.randint(1, 2)
    if result == 1:
        return 'HEADS'
    else:
        return 'TAILS'

items: Leave two empty lines and add the self-test, then two more empty lines and the guard:

content.code:
def main():
    """Quick self-test for the library."""
    print('Testing function_library.py...')
    print(f'  flip_coin() => {flip_coin()}')
    print('  Library loaded successfully.')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

content.body: This main() belongs to the library, not to your game. Because of the if __name__ guard, it runs only when you run function_library.py itself, never when lab-2-2.py imports it. Every function in the library gets a docstring, the same as main() in your lab.

Run the library by itself. With function_library.py open, click Run (or type python3 function_library.py in the terminal). The coin is random, so you'll get one of these. Run it a few times until you've seen both:

content.body: Two more functions: roll_d20(), which rolls a 20-sided die, and check_percentage(), which says yes a certain percent of the time. Together with flip_coin(), that's every random thing your game needs.

check_percentage() takes a parameter: the percent you pass in when you call it. check_percentage(30) is true about 30 times out of 100. One function, any chance you want, and the game never needs to know how the dice work.

def roll_d20():
    """
    Roll a 20-sided die.

    Returns:
        int: Random number from 1 to 20
    """
    return random.randint(D20_MIN, D20_MAX)

items: Under roll_d20(), the same way, add check_percentage(). It rolls 1 to 100 and returns True when the roll is at or under the percent:

content.code:
def check_percentage(percent):
    """
    Return True a certain percentage of the time.

    Args:
        percent (int): The percentage chance (0-100)

    Returns:
        bool: True if the roll is within the percentage
    """
    roll = random.randint(1, 100)
    return roll <= percent

content.body: No more typing your roll. lab-2-2.py imports your library and calls roll_d20() every turn. To test, you'll pin the roll to a fixed number.

Random code is hard to test: every run is different, so you can't compare it to an expected output. A pin fixes that. You comment out the random line and put a fixed value right below it, so the program does the same thing every time. When you're done testing, you put the real line back. CodeGrade does its own version of this with fixed dice, and it tests every outcome.

content.quote: Here's the hole from Lab 1.3, closed for good: nobody types a 30 anymore. And here's my favorite testing trick, which you'll use the rest of the semester. Pin the dice. Run the case you want, on purpose, as many times as you want. A tester who waits for luck to show them the bug is going to wait a long time.

content.body: Texas roads have surprises. On every turn where you haven't arrived yet, there's a 30% chance of a hazard: one of three, picked at random. A coin flip decides whether you escape it. The report's STATISTICS block counts them.

This is your library at work: check_percentage() decides whether a hazard happens, and flip_coin() decides how it ends. The hazard check goes inside the else that prints the second Miles remaining line, so it only runs on turns where you're still on the road. The counters work like Lab 2.1's: per-leg counts start at 0 before the inner loop, and the game totals add them after each leg. Because the check is inside the inner loop, the Galveston leg gets hazards too, with no extra code.

content.quote: I lost a whole evening once because a hazard fired on the turn I arrived. The trip was over, and the game was still rolling for trouble. Put the check inside the else, and that can't happen.
